<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
# Review: *Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources*

This is a good synthesis. It keeps source 3's documented corrections while rejecting its overreach, it carries forward source 2's distinction between discretionary and coverage-bound work, and it reaches a conditional conclusion: per hour, yes, moderately; per worker, no; in coverage-bound work, no. The "What the body leaves open" section is honest. Section 3.2 deserves particular credit for putting per-worker output alongside per-hour output, because it shows that "more productive per hour" and "more output" come apart.

Its weaknesses come mainly from two sources. Some errors in the source papers are carried through uncorrected. And the briefing doesn't recognise how much the five sources overlap. Together these make the bottom line more confident than the evidence allows.

## Main problems

### 1. The five sources are not independent

The briefing treats agreement across sources as corroboration. The underlying data, however, are largely shared:

| Source | What it draws on |
|---|---|
| 3 | A re-analysis of source 1's data |
| 4 | Includes source 1 (Halden) and source 2 (Varden) among its 23 studies |
| 5 | The same Varden offices as source 2, plus a subset of source 1's organisations |

So "five sources" amounts to two primary datasets plus a meta-analysis that contains both of them. When the meta-analysis subgroups "converge on 8 to 10%" and Varden also lands there, Varden is being partly counted twice. The meta-analysis subgroups also overlap heavily with each other, a point raised in the review of source 4.

The briefing should say this plainly. In particular, the strongest evidence for the 8–10% figure is a single county, with seven treated and seven control case-processing offices. The remaining rows of Table 1 largely corroborate it rather than replicate it.

### 2. The decline is still quoted across two different measures

Section 1 says the gain "declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)". This repeats source 5's own inconsistency: 12.5% is a timesheet figure at nine months, and 8.5% is a log figure at 24 months. On the same timesheet measure, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, a decline of about a fifth.

Two further qualifications belong in the briefing:

- **The decline was not tested.** The 9-month and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily.
- **The control arm changed.** Two control offices held their own meeting audit at month 15 and raised their output per hour. That lowers the measured treatment effect from month 15 onward. It could account for roughly half of the 2.7-point decline.

### 3. Log hours measure time on cases, not total working time

The briefing describes log-measured hours as the strictest standard. But time logged in the case-management system captures time spent working on cases. It leaves out meetings, email and phone calls. So "+8.5% per log hour" means output per hour spent on cases, not output per hour worked.

This also affects the mediation result. Meeting time does not appear in that denominator. So "about half the gain comes from fewer meetings" implies that fewer meetings made case work itself more efficient, perhaps through fewer interruptions. That differs from the plain reading that meetings were removed as low-value time.

### 4. The meetings figure is too confident for a bottom-line claim

Section 3.4 and the bottom line both state "about half of it through fewer meetings" without qualification. That figure comes from one registered mediation analysis, with these limits:

- **It is not out-of-sample.** It was run on the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis in the first place.
- **The effective sample is small.** It rests on 14 offices, so confidence intervals from office-month data are probably too narrow.
- **Meeting cuts were not randomised.** The analysis depends on an assumption of no unmeasured confounding. For example, offices with better managers may have cut more meetings and also improved for other reasons.

A defensible version would be: "in the one trial that tested it, about half the gain was associated with fewer meetings".

### 5. The ranges in Section 3.2 don't follow from the arithmetic as stated

Section 3.2 says hours fall 11–14% and output per hour rises 8–10%, so output per worker is 2–4% lower. Combining the ends of those two ranges gives a wider result:

| Hours cut | Per-hour gain | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|
| 11% | +10% | 0.89 × 1.10 = 0.979, about −2% |
| 14% | +8% | 0.86 × 1.08 = 0.929, about −7% |

The 2–4% figure is supported by direct estimates: −3.4% in Varden at 24 months, and −2.7% for controlled discretionary studies in the meta-analysis. The briefing should cite those directly, rather than present 2–4% as derived from the stated ranges.

The slogan "same output in four days is close to true" is also misleading. Staff were not working four days' worth of hours. Actual hours fell only 11–14%, because of overtime and longer working days. "Nearly the same output from about 12% fewer hours" is accurate.

### 6. Table 1 does not show what it claims

The table is described as "ordered by strength of design", and the text says "estimates fall as designs strengthen". The rows do not show this:

- **The order is not monotonic.** It runs 11.8 → 10.8 → 13.4, and the 9-month randomised estimate (12.5%) is higher than several weaker designs.
- **Meta-analytic rows are mixed in with single studies.** These are syntheses, not designs, and they contain the single studies listed around them.
- **The counter-work row doesn't belong.** That +6.7% is mostly higher utilisation: fewer staff serving the same demand, with the public absorbing the difference through longer waits. It also sits in a table whose conclusion is about discretionary work.

The table would be clearer split by type of work, with one like-for-like measure per row.

### 7. Sickness and resignations are presented as more solid than they are

"Real benefits … in every source" glosses over three problems:

- **Exposure.** A shorter schedule mechanically reduces the number of days on which sickness can be recorded. A four-day week alone predicts roughly a 20% fall. None of the sources adjusts for this.
- **Halden's design.** The 36% figure comes from an uncontrolled pilot that compared a likely winter baseline with a summer pilot period.
- **Precision.** Resignation estimates are imprecise in Varden and uncontrolled in Halden. The meta-analysis result is a vote count.

These outcomes probably do improve, but "real benefits" should be qualified, and the 27–36% range should not be read as the size of the effect.

## Gaps for a policy audience

**Cost.** A working group will want to know what this costs, and the briefing doesn't say:

- **Discretionary work:** pay is maintained and output per worker falls 2–4%, so the labour cost per unit of output rises by roughly 2–4%. Overtime adds to that.
- **Coverage-bound work:** Varden estimated a 9% rise in cost per contact to restore service, and that came from a single county.

The "about 12% more staff" figure in Section 3.3 is likewise one county's estimate. It should not be read as a general one.

**Further open questions.** Section 4 should also list:

- **Backlogs.** Varden never reported backlog size or time to decision, so a stable count of cases closed could hide a growing queue.
- **Few-cluster inference.** No source corrected for having only 7 offices per arm.
- **Halden's attrition.** The discrepancy in withdrawal timing found by source 3 has still not been answered by the Halden authors.
- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 Halden organisations with output records replied at 24 months. If the nine that didn't reply include more reverters, 3 of 14 understates the reversion rate.

## Smaller points

- **Source 4.** "Its claim of no decay was wrong" should read "unsupported". One controlled study showing a modest decline does not show the general claim to be false. It shows that the evidence offered for it could not test the question.
- **Source 3.** "Those further claims do not survive" is right for "entirely an artifact" and for "zero by month ten". The milder version of the novelty argument gets partial support, though, since some fading did occur. Saying so would be fairer.
- **Source 1.** "Established that many organisations … could cut hours" should note that some organisations withdrew after the schedule had started.

## A suggested bottom line

> In discretionary work, reducing scheduled hours by a fifth at full pay reduced actual hours by about 12% and, in the strongest single trial, raised output per hour by about 10% at two years, down from about 12% in the first year. Output per worker was 2–4% lower and unit labour cost correspondingly higher. In that trial, about half the gain was associated with fewer recurring meetings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fell unless staff were added. The evidence rests heavily on one public-sector employer, and whether reorganising work without cutting hours would deliver much of the gain is untested.

I can revise Table 1 along the lines suggested, or draft a short cost annex for the working group.
